fixes.explanation: That's the reason the verse gives. Moses retells what the LORD said about those years: no bread, no wine, no strong drink, and then the LORD's reason, “…so that you might know that I am the LORD your God.” Moses doesn't leave us guessing at a reason. Simple and clear, friend.

That sounds like a reasonable guess, friend, but the verse never says it. Moses retells the LORD's words, and the reason is “…so that you might know that I am the LORD your God.” Battles do come up in this passage, but not as the reason for this. I'd stick with what the text says.

It's a nice thought, but the text doesn't say that. Moses gives one reason, and the LORD is the one speaking it: “…so that you might know that I am the LORD your God.” I'm not going to add one the Bible doesn't. That's like adding sprinkles to a recipe that never asked for them.

True! Moses says, “So keep and follow the words of this covenant, that you may prosper in all you do.” A command AND the reason, in one breath. Most of my old kitchen instructions never came with a reason. I just got a pat on the handle and a "press harder, Dorin."

They're actually in, friend. Moses names “…the foreigners in your camps who cut your wood and draw your water…” in the list of those standing before the LORD (Deuteronomy 29:10–11). The list is for those who enter the covenant, and they're on it.

Right, they are not left out. Moses lists them among those standing before the LORD: “…the foreigners in your camps who cut your wood and draw your water…” The list is there so that they may enter into the covenant (Deuteronomy 29:11–12). They're named right in the verse.

Moab is where they're standing, friend, so I see the pull. But the verse doesn't name the people of Moab. It names those standing there “…in the presence of the LORD our God, as well as with those who are not here today.” Stick with what the verse says.

Yes. Moses says, “You saw the abominations and idols among them made of wood and stone, of silver and gold.” They'd passed through those nations and seen it for themselves. Wood, stone, silver and gold, and every bit of it made by hand.

That's the one. Moses says, “Make sure there is no root among you that bears such poisonous and bitter fruit…” Nothing sweet about it. He's talking about a heart that turns away from the LORD, so it's a serious picture, friend. I think that's why he keeps it so plain.

That's the opposite of what Moses says. The root bears “…such poisonous and bitter fruit…” The root is a heart turning away from the LORD (Deuteronomy 29:18), so this is a serious warning. Nothing sweet or plentiful in it.

Good thinking, but small and hidden isn't what Moses says. He says the root “…bears such poisonous and bitter fruit…” Poison and bitterness are the words he picks, and they're about a heart turning from the LORD. It's a serious warning, so I'd keep his words exactly.

That's what Moses says. The LORD “…will blot out his name from under heaven” It's a heavy thing to read, friend, and I think it hurts a little. Moses says it in the middle of a warning about turning away from the LORD (Deuteronomy 29:18–20).

That's what Moses says: “All its soil will be a burning waste of sulfur and salt, unsown and unproductive, with no plant growing on it…” It's a hard picture, and Moses compares it to Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, which the LORD overthrew (Deuteronomy 29:23). I think this is one to read slowly.

The verse doesn't narrow it down like that, friend. Moses says the revealed things belong “…to us and to our children forever…” and the word "alone" isn't in there. Moses says "us," so he counts himself in with the whole crowd and their children. That's a wide door, and nobody's checking a list at it.
Proclaiming sounds loud and good, friend, and I like loud. But the verse says the revealed things are theirs “…so that we may follow all the words of this law.” The word is follow.
